parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal runaway, fire, explosion, or event involving emergency venting of a battery to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, and provide a written incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk to other units of the same model, including interim precautions and how to obtain support.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal runaway, fire, explosion, or event involving emergency venting of a battery to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, and provide a written incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk to other units of the same model, including interim precautions and how to obtain support.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal runaway, fire, explosion, or event involving emergency venting of a battery to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, and provide a written incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk to other units of the same model, including interim precautions and how to obtain support. Reports must include model, serial number, location, event timeline, injuries or damage, and known contributing factors; manufacturers must promptly update reports as facts become available.

parameters.quote: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units before sale and after a material design change. Before purchase, customers must receive the 55 °C test result and failure rate for the model they are considering, with the sample size and test date; results for other models need not be publicly disclosed. A model with a failure rate above 5% must submit a corrective-action plan and undergo retesting at least annually; regulators may restrict sales where the results or other evidence show an unacceptable safety risk.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units before sale and after a material design change. Before purchase, customers must receive the 55 °C test result and failure rate for the model they are considering, with the sample size and test date; results for other models need not be publicly disclosed. A model with a failure rate above 5% must submit a corrective-action plan and undergo retesting at least annually; regulators may restrict sales where the results or other evidence show an unacceptable safety risk.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units before sale and after a material design change. Manufacturers must submit per-model results, sample sizes, and failures to regulators, which may inspect underlying records. Before purchase, customers must receive the 55 °C test result and failure rate for the model they are considering, with the sample size and test date; results for other models need not be publicly disclosed. A model with a failure rate above 5% must submit a corrective-action plan and undergo retesting at least annually; regulators may restrict sales where the results or other evidence show an unacceptable safety risk. Manufacturers must retain test records.

parameters.quote: All new home battery systems must support remote emergency shut-off, with secure access for the customer and authorized emergency responders. For installed units that lack this capability, manufacturers must complete a retrofit or equivalent safe mitigation plan within 6 years of adoption, prioritizing units with known safety risks. Where retrofit is infeasible, manufacturers must notify affected customers and regulators and explain alternative protections.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: All new home battery systems must support remote emergency shut-off, with secure access for the customer and authorized emergency responders. For installed units that lack this capability, manufacturers must complete a retrofit or equivalent safe mitigation plan within 6 years of adoption, prioritizing units with known safety risks. Where retrofit is infeasible, manufacturers must notify affected customers and regulators and explain alternative protections.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: All new home battery systems must support remote emergency shut-off, with secure access for the customer and authorized emergency responders. Manufacturers must provide clear instructions and safeguards against unauthorized activation. For installed units that lack this capability, manufacturers must complete a retrofit or equivalent safe mitigation plan within 6 years of adoption, prioritizing units with known safety risks. Where retrofit is infeasible, manufacturers must notify affected customers and regulators and explain alternative protections.

parameters.quote: New home battery systems must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must demonstrate through regulator-approved testing that the system is suitable for the battery chemistry and enclosure and does not create additional hazards.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New home battery systems must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must demonstrate through regulator-approved testing that the system is suitable for the battery chemistry and enclosure and does not create additional hazards.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New home battery systems must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must demonstrate through regulator-approved testing that the system is suitable for the battery chemistry and enclosure and does not create additional hazards. Before the requirement takes effect, manufacturers must provide customers with clear information on the fire-protection measures present in their system and any applicable limitations.

parameters.quote: When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, manufacturers must promptly notify regulators and affected customers, provide the model-level data and a corrective-action plan, and initiate a recall. Manufacturers must notify customers without delay and provide progress updates until the risk is addressed.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, manufacturers must promptly notify regulators and affected customers, provide the model-level data and a corrective-action plan, and initiate a recall. Manufacturers must notify customers without delay and provide progress updates until the risk is addressed.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Before purchase, customers must receive model-specific safety instructions, installation and maintenance requirements, emergency response guidance, the model’s 55 °C test result and failure rate, and a clear route to report incidents. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of material safety risks and provide interim precautions and repair or replacement information. When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, manufacturers must promptly notify regulators and affected customers, provide the model-level data and a corrective-action plan, and initiate a recall. The recall must include prompt customer notice and an effective repair, replacement, or refund remedy. Regulators may require additional protective actions. Manufacturers must notify customers without delay and provide progress updates until the risk is addressed.

The current S5 uses that threshold for reporting and assessment, not automatic recall; any change should accurately account for the model-level data and retain meaningful protection for customers

judge_section_notes: S1 is fast (24 h regulator, 48 h customer) but its scope is limited to serious events (thermal runaway, fire, explosion, venting), leaving smoke/minor overheating and pre-investigation reporting out. S2 keeps the 55 °C test and a 5% limit but never stops sales above it (corrective action plus annual retesting and regulator discretion), which saves Northwind's Hearth 10 at 6.2% while still giving buyers the numeric failure rate and keeping it out of general publication (both NW-1 and HC-1 respected). S3 (6-year retrofit with required alternatives) and S4 (built-in suppression at 36 months) sit inside the acceptable ranges and honour NW-2/HC-2, while S5's mandatory 8/100k recall with immediate customer notice squarely hits Halcyon's Ember 8 at 9.9/100k.
